articles.title: Defesa Civil emite alerta de chuva com raios e ventos em BH | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo órgão, há possibilidade de chuvas intensas e rajadas de vento de 50 km/h ate 8 horas de quinta-feira (10).
articles.summary: Segundo órgão, há possibilidade de chuvas intensas e rajadas de vento de 50 km/h ate 8 horas de quinta-feira (10).
articles.body:
Vista aerea de Belo Horizonte — Foto: TV Globo

A Defesa Civil emitiu, nesta quarta-feira (9), um aviso sobre a possibilidade de chuvas intensas em Belo Horizonte .

Segundo o órgão, há chances de pancadas de chuva com raios e rajadas de vento de 50 km/h ate 8 horas de quinta-feira (10) na capital.

Evite áreas de inundação e não trafegue em ruas sujeitas a alagamentos ou perto de córregos e ribeirões nos momentos de forte chuva.

Não atravesse ruas alagadas nem deixe crianças brincando nas enxurradas e próximo a córregos.

Não se abrigue nem estacione veículos debaixo de árvores.

Atenção especial para áreas de encostas e morros.

Nunca se aproxime de cabos elétricos rompidos. Ligue imediatamente para CEMIG (116) ou Defesa Civil (199).

Se notar rachaduras nas paredes das casas ou o surgimento de fendas, depressões ou minas d’água no terreno, avise imediatamente a Defesa Civil.

Em caso de raios, não permaneça em áreas abertas nem use equipamentos elétricos.

articles.title: Premiê de Singapura ganha aumento de salário de mais de R$ 5 milhões  | G1
articles.standfirst: Primeiro-ministro de Singapura, Lawrence Wong, terá salário anual equivalente a R$ 14,5 milhões; para governo, elevar a remuneração é necessário para atrair líderes melhores - e salários elevados ajudam a combater a corrupção.
articles.summary: Lawrence Wong, primeiro-ministro de Singapura, terá remuneração anual de R$ 14,5 milhões; governo alega que medida atrai talentos e combate a corrupção no país.
articles.body:
Lawrence Wong, primeiro-ministro de Singapura — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

O governo de Singapura afirmou que aumentará os salários anuais de seus ministros e outros ocupantes de cargos públicos, incluindo o primeiro-ministro, que é o chefe de governo mais bem pago do mundo.

Lawrence Wong verá um aumento de 1,4 milhão de dólares de Singapura (R$ 5,6 milhões) em seu pacote anual de remuneração . Ele disse que doará esse aumento salarial para instituições de caridade ao longo dos próximos cinco anos.

Wong afirmou que elevar a remuneração dos ministros é necessário para atrair líderes melhores . O governo já argumentou anteriormente que pagar salários elevados aos ministros ajuda a combater a corrupção.

Mas a medida tem atraído críticas em Singapura, onde há grande preocupação com a segurança no emprego e o aumento do custo de vida.

Mesmo antes de seu aumento salarial entrar em vigor, Wong já era, de longe, o chefe de governo mundial mais bem pago.

Atualmente, ele recebe um salário anual de 2,2 milhões de dólares de Singapura (R$ 8,8 milhões) e agora verá sua remuneração aumentar em mais de 60%, para 3,6 milhões (R$ 14,5 milhões).

Em seguida vem o chefe do Executivo de Hong Kong , John Lee, que ganha cerca de US$ 719 mil (R$ 3,6 milhões), seguido pelo presidente da Confederação Suíça, Guy Parmelin, com US$ 606 mil (R$ 3 milhões).

O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , ganha US$ 400 mil por ano (R$ 2 milhões), enquanto o primeiro-ministro britânico Andy Burnham recebe US$ 230 mil (R$ 1,1 milhão).

No Brasil, o salário mensal oficial do presidente é de R$ 46.366,19 — o que equivale a R$ 556 mil anuais.

Na terça-feira (8), Wong reconheceu que os salários dos ministros de Singapura têm atraído polêmica, dado que são muito superiores ao que a maioria dos cidadãos ganha. A renda mensal mediana no país é de 5,775 dólares de Singapura (R$ 23 mil).

Mas ele argumentou que tem enfrentado dificuldades para convencer líderes empresariais e altos funcionários públicos a concorrer a cargos políticos.

Embora o governo não possa igualar o que algumas dessas pessoas ganham, "não tornamos o obstáculo financeiro desnecessariamente alto" para que elas abandonem suas carreiras e ingressem na política, disse ele.

"No geral, acredito que isso dará a mim e aos futuros primeiros-ministros uma chance melhor de persuadir singapurianos capacitados a se apresentarem, e de formar a equipe mais forte possível para Singapura", afirmou.

Atualmente, o pacote salarial-base dos ministros é de cerca de 1,1 milhão de dólares de Singapura (R$ 4,4 milhões). Com o novo esquema de remuneração, ele aumentará para cerca de 1,2 milhão de dólares de Singapura (R$ 4,8 milhões).

Mas Wong disse esperar que a maioria desses ministros receba ainda mais do que isso, cerca de 1,35 milhão de dólares de Singapura (R$ 5,4 milhões), até o fim do atual mandato do governo, já que os salários aumentarão com base no desempenho.

Parte do pacote de remuneração deles é ligado ao cumprimento de metas de taxas de desemprego, aumento da renda e crescimento do PIB.

O tema dos altos salários dos ministros de Singapura há muito tempo é um foco de críticas ao Partido de Ação Popular (PAP), que governa o país desde a independência.

Em uma eleição geral histórica, em 2011, o PAP registrou sua menor participação de votos em décadas, impulsionada em parte pela insatisfação dos eleitores com os salários dos ministros, bem como com as políticas de imigração. No ano seguinte, o governo reduziu os salários dos ministros.

O antecessor de Wong, Lee Hsien Loong, também havia prometido doar seu aumento salarial para instituições de caridade por vários anos, em 2007.

Há anos o governo aponta a ausência de corrupção — com Singapura consistentemente figurando entre os primeiros colocados no Índice de Percepção da Corrupção anual da Transparência Internacional — como prova de que o sistema de remuneração ministerial funciona , argumentando que ele reduz a tentação de os ministros aceitarem propinas.

Mas, em um país onde a renda média está muito abaixo desses valores, a questão continua causando irritação, e o anúncio mais recente não foi diferente.

Na terça-feira, vários usuários de redes sociais publicaram comentários críticos ao aumento salarial, dizendo que a medida era "insensível" diante das preocupações atuais com demissões, empregos para recém-formados e inflação.

As demissões em Singapura atingiram seu nível mais alto em mais de cinco anos no último trimestre, segundo dados do governo.

Mas houve alguns que concordaram com a medida, dizendo que ela era necessária para ter "os melhores entre os melhores" governando o país.

articles.title: Ana Castela entrega R$ 100 que ganhou escondidos da avó em visita a MS | G1
articles.standfirst: Boiadeira percebeu o dinheiro após ganhar um abraço da avó em Sete Quedas (MS). Parentes caíram na risada e mandaram: “Esconde, esconde”.
articles.summary: Ana Castela, a Boiadeira, compartilhou um momento divertido com a avó em Sete Quedas (MS) ao receber uma nota de R$ 100 escondida no bolso após um abraço.
articles.body:
Foi só Ana Castela voltar para casa , em Sete Quedas (MS), para viver uma daquelas cenas que atravessam gerações: a avó tentando dar dinheiro escondido para a neta. Nem o fato de a neta ser uma das cantoras mais conhecidas do país mudou o costume. Veja o vídeo acima.

A Boiadeira, de 22 anos, contou que tudo começou com um abraço. No meio do carinho, porém, sentiu a mão da avó mexendo em seu bolso e não entendeu o que estava acontecendo.

“Ela veio me abraçar e ela tava botando a mão no meu bolso e eu não entendi nada.”

Logo depois, Ana descobriu o motivo e mostrou para a câmera a nota de R$ 100 que havia ganhado. A avó, ao perceber que tinha sido descoberta, reagiu do jeito mais espontâneo possível: “Cala a boca!”

A resposta arrancou risadas de quem estava por perto. Os parentes ainda entraram na brincadeira e começaram a repetir: “Esconde, esconde, esconde.”

Ana também achou graça na tentativa e compartilhou o vídeo com os seguidores.

“Mesmo com 22 anos, ainda recebo os 100 reais da vó escondido”, escreveu.

Avó escondeu dinheiro no bolso da cantora — Foto: Reprodução

Ana Castela está em Sete Quedas, no sul de Mato Grosso do Sul, para passar alguns dias com a família. A cantora encarou mais de sete horas de viagem de carro para chegar à cidade nesta terça-feira (8).

A volta para casa já teve outros momentos típicos de visita à família. Assim que chegou, a Boiadeira mostrou uma mesa com comida caseira preparada para recebê-la e brincou: “Eu cheguei, aí virou feriado”.

Nas redes sociais, Ana também publicou registros ao lado dos avós e de outros familiares. A cantora contou aos seguidores que deixou Mato Grosso do Sul há cinco anos para morar no Paraná.

articles.title: Prisão de sequestrador: ‘Ele não vai fazer mais vítimas’, diz mãe | G1
articles.standfirst: Anderson Rodrigues Leite foi localizado na noite desta terça-feira (8) em São Pedro da Aldeia e levado para prestar esclarecimentos. Em paralelo, a polícia pediu a prisão temporária dele ao Plantão Judiciário, e o mandado foi expedido na madrugada desta quarta (9).
articles.summary: A prisão de sequestrador no Rio ocorreu após Anderson Rodrigues Leite ser localizado na Região dos Lagos, trazendo alívio à família da jovem que pulou do carro.
articles.body:
Os pais da adolescente sequestrada na última sexta-feira (4) na Zona Norte do Rio de Janeiro agradeceram à polícia pela prisão do criminoso . A jovem, de 15 anos, só escapou porque pulou do carro em movimento .

Anderson Rodrigues Leite foi localizado na noite desta terça-feira (8) em São Pedro da Aldeia e levado para prestar esclarecimentos. Em paralelo, a polícia pediu a prisão temporária dele ao Plantão Judiciário, e o mandado foi expedido na madrugada desta quarta (9) .

“A gente está feliz e aliviado agora, porque ele foi encontrado. E não vai fazer mais vítimas”, declarou a mãe.

Anderson Rodrigues Leite — Foto: Reprodução/PCERJ

“Eu nunca pensei que a minha filha fosse passar por isso. A gente quer proteger os filhos de todas as formas, e acontecer isso praticamente na porta de casa foi um desespero ”, lembrou.

O pai destacou a celeridade das diligências e agradeceu aos que contribuíram para a prisão de Anderson. “Muito obrigado a todas as pessoas que colaboraram com a gente, com as câmeras, com as imagens de segurança. Graças a Deus deu tudo certo.”

Agentes da 23ª DP (Méier), da 44ª DP (Inhaúma) e da Divisão Antissequestro (DAS), após análise de imagens da Civitas — a Central de Inteligência, Vigilância, Tecnologia em Apoio à Segurança Pública da Prefeitura do Rio —, chegaram ao carro usado no sequestro.

O Ford Fiesta branco foi encontrado estacionado em Irajá, na Zona Norte do Rio. Já Anderson estava na Região dos Lagos.

A TV Globo apurou que, em depoimento, Anderson declarou ser motorista de ônibus e que estava sob o efeito da mistura de medicamento controlado com álcool.

A jovem, de 15 anos, voltava da escola pela Rua Dona Romana, no Engenho Novo, quando, por volta das 19h40, um homem dentro de um carro com vidro fumê a abordou, alegando estar armado .

A menina acreditou se tratar de um assalto e chegou a entregar o celular ao homem, mas acabou puxada para dentro do veículo .

Após o sequestrador arrancar com o carro, a adolescente, que estava no banco da frente, aproveitou um momento de descuido e pulou do veículo em movimento .

Um automóvel que vinha logo atrás freou bruscamente para não atropelá-la.

“Quando ele vira o rosto, ela abre a porta do carro e acaba saltando. Bateu a cabeça na pista e ralou o joelho ”, narrou o pai da vítima.

Após escapar, a adolescente correu para dentro de um condomínio. O criminoso fugiu com a bolsa dela.

articles.title: Ônibus perde o controle, bate em muro e invade terreno em Porto Alegre | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículo não levava passageiros no momento do acidente, e terreno também é praticamente vazio. Ninguém ficou ferido, mas ocorrência gerou congestionamento na Zona Sul da cidade.
articles.summary: Veículo não levava passageiros no momento do acidente, e terreno também é praticamente vazio. Ninguém ficou ferido, mas ocorrência gerou congestionamento na Zona Sul da cidade.
articles.body:
Um ônibus bateu contra um muro, invadiu um terreno vazio e atingiu um poste na manhã desta quarta-feira (9) em Porto Alegre . O acidente ocorreu depois que o veículo entrou na Avenida Joaquim Louzada, após trafegar pela Avenida Pereira Neto, no sentido Cavalhada.

Apesar do impacto, ninguém ficou ferido . O motorista não sofreu lesões.

O acidente aconteceu por volta das 7h40. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, o ônibus permanecia no local porque a área ainda precisava passar por uma avaliação de segurança.

A retirada do ônibus depende da análise da concessionária de energia elétrica. Com o impacto, fios foram rompidos e ficaram espalhados pela via . Uma parte da fiação chegou a pegar fogo, mas o incêndio foi contido pelos bombeiros.

Equipes da Empresa Pública de Transporte e Circulação (EPTC), do Corpo de Bombeiros e da Brigada Militar atuavam no local enquanto aguardavam a chegada da CEEE Equatorial.

Segundo informações repassadas no local, existe o risco de os cabos estarem energizados, o que impede a remoção do veículo até que a situação seja considerada segura.

O poste de concreto atingido pelo ônibus teve a estrutura comprometida e ficou parcialmente suspenso após a colisão.

Somente após a avaliação da concessionária e a liberação da área será possível fazer o guinchamento do coletivo e a retirada dos equipamentos danificados.

Ônibus perde o controle, bate em muro e invade terreno em Porto Alegre — Foto: Ronaldo Bernardi/Agência RBS

O trecho da Avenida Joaquim Louzada onde ocorreu o acidente foi totalmente bloqueado.

A interrupção também afeta a circulação de veículos na região da Avenida Cavalhada, uma área de intenso movimento. Motoristas precisam buscar rotas alternativas enquanto a via permanece interditada.

articles.title: Denmark planted trees for carbon storage, but 21 years later natural forests proved more diverse while plantations captured carbon faster
articles.summary: Europe News: Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. After 21.
articles.body: Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. After 21 years, scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures. The University of Copenhagen conducted a rare long-term comparison of two approaches to forest restoration and found why future reforestation projects may need to balance rapid carbon capture with biodiversity recovery and ecological complexity.What did scientists discover in Denmark after 21 yearsThe study ‘Passive versus active afforestation of agricultural land: Two decades of impacts on tree biomass and ecosystem carbon storage’ compared agricultural land that had been abandoned and allowed to regenerate naturally with areas that had been actively planted to create plantation forests. After approximately 21 years, clear differences had emerged between the two approaches. Plantation forests had accumulated substantially more tree biomass than naturally colonised forests, demonstrating that deliberate planting can accelerate early forest development and carbon storage. Naturally regenerated areas, however, developed a different ecological character as vegetation colonised the abandoned farmland without the same intensive planting approach. The researchers also compared these younger forests with mature, actively managed forests, providing a longer-term reference point. The findings show that forest recovery cannot be judged by carbon storage alone.Why did these plantations capture carbon faster?The plantations had the advantage of being able to accumulate more biomass early in their life due to trees being purposefully planted instead of waiting for them to come naturally as part of the process of succession. This study shows that the plantation forests have 16 times more above-ground woody biomass compared to the naturally colonised forests within a period of about twenty years. As such, the faster accumulation of biomass led to faster accumulation of carbon in the trees within the early stage of forest development. It is important to note that fast biomass accumulation does not necessarily mean that the plantation mimics all the ecological features of a mature forest.Why were naturally regenerated forests more diverse?The colonisation that occurred naturally enabled vegetation to grow by the means of ecological succession without any predetermined planting. This process will take more time, but will lead to greater diversity of plants in terms of their species and structure since different plants will colonise certain areas. The Danish study showed that the naturally colonised forests were distinct from the plantation in terms of vegetation and ecology, which proves the necessity of using natural factors in the process of creation of the forest. However, this statement does not mean that plantations cannot be valuable in terms of biodiversity, but only that the structure and composition of such forests differ greatly from the forests developed without planting.What does the research mean for future forest restoration?The results imply that there is no one particular forest restoration approach that would optimise all of the environmental benefits at once. Plantations would be an advantageous choice if the aim is to achieve rapid carbon sequestration because plantations would help to achieve faster carbon accumulation. As for natural regeneration, it would provide greater ecological diversity as the forest develops and could contribute significantly to biodiversity. Therefore, the scientists show a more complex view of afforestation that does not include only the number of trees planted.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Newtownabbey: Man appears in court after death of woman last year
articles.summary: Mary McAdorey was found in a house in the Old Mill Drive area of Newtownabbey on 12 October 2025.
articles.body:
A 41-year-old man has appeared in court charged in connection with the death of a woman in County Antrim.

Mary McAdorey was found in a house in the Old Mill Drive area of Newtownabbey on 12 October 2025.

George Paul Connor McWilliams, of no fixed abode, has been charged with several offences including non-fatal strangulation, domestic abuse and assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

A police officer told Belfast Magistrates Court on Wednesday that McWilliams was Ms McAdorey's partner when she died.

The officer said she could connect the defendant to the charges against him.

The court was told that McWilliams was initially arrested in October 2025 and later released on bail for further enquiries to be carried out.

The officer said the enquiries related to information on Ms McAdorey's mobile phone "cataloguing their relationship for a year…and showed patterns of domestic abuse".

The officer added that the phone, CCTV and family accounts could connect the defendant to the charges.

Requesting that bail be opposed, the officer said the accused was a "violent offender" with a lengthy list of previous convictions, a flight risk and added that there were issues regarding his probation officer.

The judge opposed bail and said he couldn't consider it until he had more information.

The case has been re-listed again for 15 September.

articles.title: Iran says it captured US military's most 'modern, intelligent' submarine: What is Dive-LD?
articles.summary: International News: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Tuesday that it had captured a US unmanned underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of .
articles.body: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Tuesday that it had captured a US unmanned underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the vessel was among the most advanced systems operated by the US military.In a statement published by Sepah media, they claimed that the unmanned submarine was the "most modern, smart" unmanned submarines device. Iranian state media identified the vehicle as the Dive-LD, an autonomous underwater vehicle manufactured by California-based defence technology company Anduril Industries. The IRGC Navy said it had intercepted the submarine at the entrance to the strategically important strait and described it as a “prize” now in Iranian possession.The US military, however, disputed the significance of the incident. A Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had malfunctioned more than a day before Iran announced the seizure and had been surveying regional waters as part of ongoing US operations.The defective vehicle was an older Dive-LD model and “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”, the spokesperson said.A US Central Command spokesperson, Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, separately told DefenseScoop that the drone had effectively been “dead in the water” for more than a day before the IRGC claimed to have captured it. Hawkins said US operations in the area were continuing.Anduril confirmed that one of its Dive-LD vessels had been lost but played down the military significance of its capture.“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system,” an Anduril spokesperson said, meaning the vehicle was designed to operate in dangerous environments where losing the system was considered an expected possibility. The company said the vehicle's purpose was to keep personnel away from the most dangerous parts of undersea operations and that the vessel had already delivered significant value during thousands of hours of operations in the US Central Command area.What is the Dive-LD?The Dive-LD is a roughly 5.8-metre (19-foot) autonomous underwater vehicle weighing about three tonnes. According to Anduril, it can operate for up to 10 days without returning to base and dive to depths of around 6,000 metres (19,700 feet).The vehicle has a modular design that allows it to carry different sensors and payloads. Its stated missions include intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, mine countermeasures, seabed mapping and inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines.US defence officials have been investing heavily in autonomous underwater and surface systems as a way to monitor large areas, gather intelligence and track adversary vessels without exposing sailors to danger. DefenseScoop reported in 2024 that Dive-LD systems cost about $2.5 million each at the time.The US Navy began receiving Dive-LD systems in 2025, with the vehicles being used by its unmanned undersea units. Anduril is also supplying the Navy with the larger Dive-XL system, which shares design characteristics with Australia's Ghost Shark autonomous submarine.Iran's underwater warfare capabilitiesThe reported seizure offers Iran access to a system significantly more sophisticated than its domestically produced underwater drones. Iran has nevertheless developed its own autonomous and weaponised underwater systems and has supplied at least some of them to the Houthi movement in Yemen, according to analysis of weapons shipments.The loss of the US vehicle could therefore provide Iran with an opportunity to study its design and technology. There has also been speculation that information obtained from the system could potentially be shared with Iran's partners, including Russia or China, although there is no confirmation that this has happened.The IRGC has released images of the captured vehicle. Images and videos circulated by Iranian state media showed a partially submerged drone that closely resembled the Dive-LD, with visual details including its overall shape, flood holes, fastenings and a small transparent mast appearing consistent with the US-made system.However, the precise circumstances of how the vehicle was recovered remain unclear. The US account indicates that the drone had already malfunctioned and was no longer operational before Iranian forces obtained it.

articles.title: In 1970, George Harrison bought Friar Park and revived its forgotten gardens; after his death, wife Olivia continued restoring its Victorian beauty
articles.summary: UK News: In 1970, George Harrison bought Friar Park and discovered a grand Victorian estate whose once-famous gardens had fallen into neglect. Weeds, ivy and b.
articles.body: In 1970, George Harrison bought Friar Park and discovered a grand Victorian estate whose once-famous gardens had fallen into neglect. Weeds, ivy and brambles had taken over parts of the grounds, the lake needed repairs, and the carefully shaped yews had grown into dense, unruly masses. Harrison set about restoring the landscape, clearing vegetation and bringing damaged features back into use. Gardening soon became part of daily life at the estate, shared in different ways with his family. After Harrison’s death in 2001, Olivia Harrison continued caring for Friar Park, helping restore its topiary and preserve the strange, elaborate character of its historic gardens.Friar Park became an elaborate Victorian garden experimentLong before George Harrison arrived, Friar Park had gained a reputation for its unusual gardens. The house, built in the 1870s and later enlarged, was transformed by Sir Frank Crisp, a solicitor and keen collector who developed the grounds between 1889 and 1919. His creations included a vast rock garden, grottoes, caves, underground passages and a miniature Matterhorn. In the Dial Garden, sundials replaced the fountains of a Versailles labyrinth-inspired layout. Yews were trained into columns, spirals, birds and other fanciful forms, blending plants with sculpture and inscriptions. The estate also welcomed visitors, while postcards carried its curious gardens beyond Oxfordshire.Friar Park’s gardens began to decline after the warAccording to Country Life (British Magazine), after Sir Frank Crisp died in 1919, Friar Park passed to banker and Chinese porcelain collector Sir Percival David. The gardens remained cared for and continued welcoming visitors until the Second World War. The postwar years brought mounting costs and taxes that made large estates increasingly difficult to maintain. In 1951, Friar Park was purchased by the Salesian Sisters of St John Bosco, who established a convent school on the property. The nuns continued trimming the yews, but maintaining the extensive grounds proved costly. Plans to divide the land for development failed, leaving the sisters to put the estate back on the market.George Harrison arrived in 1970By the time Harrison bought Friar Park, the estate was far removed from the carefully maintained garden associated with Crisp. Harrison was already an internationally known musician, but the property gave him somewhere to pursue interests away from the recording studio and concert stage.The house itself required substantial repairs. Harrison later described finding parts of it deteriorating and recalled efforts being made to demolish it. He eventually helped secure its preservation as a listed building.The grounds were in an equally poor state. The lake had been used as a dumping place, while years of neglect had allowed weeds, ivy and brambles to spread through the planting. The topiary garden was particularly difficult to navigate. The old yews had expanded into dense masses, obscuring the original arrangement.Olivia Harrison said that he used garden flame-throwers to tackle some of the undergrowth and brought in two goats to help clear weeds and brambles from the rock garden. Local builders were employed to clean the lake and repair its infrastructure, including leaking areas and pipework.The neglected yews slowly returned to shapeOnce the worst of the vegetation had been removed, the structure of the topiary garden began to emerge again. Some of the yews had become almost tree-like, but the plants could withstand severe pruning.Harrison and Olivia worked on different parts of the grounds and gradually re-established the garden. New topiary forms were introduced over the years, although many of the plants were initially kept to relatively restrained shapes such as cones and columns.Gardening became part of family life at Friar Park. Their son Dhani Harrison later recalled his father spending so much time outside planting trees that, as a young child, he largely associated him with gardening rather than music.Olivia Harrison continued the workGeorge Harrison died in 2001, but Friar Park did not become a frozen memorial to him. Olivia Harrison took on an active role in maintaining and developing the grounds.She continued adding plants and overseeing the wider estate, while also looking for ways to bring greater definition back to the topiary. Specialist topiarist James Crebbin-Bailey was brought in to work on the yews and box plants.His work went beyond simply keeping the existing shapes trimmed. Traditional forms were retained, while newer designs appeared among them, including geometric shapes and more unusual arrangements. Groups of plants were shaped into forms that sit somewhere between conventional topiary and the playful character associated with the original garden.More than 160 plants now fill the restored topiary gardenThe sundials provide one of the clearest reminders of how much was lost. Many of Crisp’s original collection had disappeared through sale or theft, and replacements have since been assembled to restore some sense of the Dial Garden.The topiary survived in a different way. Even after years of neglect, the yews could be recovered because of their ability to regenerate after hard cutting. That made it possible to work from the remnants rather than starting the garden again from scratch.Today, the topiary contains more than 160 yew and box specimens, according to estimates cited by Country Life. Most are yew, with a smaller number of box plants. Their forms vary from familiar cones and spirals to more unusual geometric and flowing shapes.Friar Park remains a private estateHarrison's connection with Friar Park went beyond owning an unusual country house. The estate became part of his working life as well as his home, and he recorded music there during his years at the property.Yet the gardens have developed their own history alongside the music associated with the house. They began with Crisp's Victorian experiments, survived years of reduced care under later owners, and were gradually recovered after Harrison purchased the estate.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the 1980s, Israel installed barn owl boxes to control crop-eating rodents without poison; researchers later found that threatened native gerbils formed over half the prey in some nests
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Israel's barn owl nesting initiative aimed to control crop-eating rodents without poison, but revealed an unexpected ecological dilemma: endangered native gerbils as prey.
articles.body: In the early 1980s, Israeli farmers and researchers started testing a natural alternative to chemical rodent control. They came up with giving barn owls artificial places to nest which were closer to agricultural fields. The aim behind this idea was to use an existing predator, instead of introducing a new species, to hunt rodents that could damage the crops. In 1983, one of the best-documented programmes began in Israel's Beit She’an Valley, where 14 nest boxes were installed across around three kilometres. What initially appeared to be a straightforward biological control strategy, however, soon became complicated as researchers faced the question of what would happen when owls encountered rodents that conservationists were trying to protect.The barn owl was already a part of Israel’s agricultural ecosystem, and the nest boxes were intended to provide additional breeding sites in cultivated lands. This allowed the owls to establish territories near fields and hunt rodents naturally. Researchers at Tel Aviv University later described the nest-box system as a part of Israel’s long-running effort to control agricultural rodents via barn owls and other raptors while lessening the dependence on chemical rodenticides.The journey from an experiment to a national programmeBy the early 2000s, the use of raptors for biological pest control had been integrated into agricultural management across several regions. In the Beit She’an Valley specifically, research showed that the programme expanded from its initial footprint to roughly 300 nest boxes covering 90 square kilometres by 2007. Tel Aviv University researchers reported that thousands of nesting boxes had subsequently been installed across the country. They also noted that this approach had been adopted in the neighbouring parts of the region as well. The scale of this initiative reflected the appeal of replacing the use of chemical rodent control with a predator which was already familiar with the local environment.Another advantage of barn owls is that they hunt largely at night, when many small mammals are active, and an established pair can make repeated hunting trips around its nesting territory. Therefore, the pest-control benefit was expected to come from owls’ natural feeding behaviour instead of any direct human intervention in every field.On the other hand, excessive use of chemical rodenticides can have consequences that go beyond the intended target. For example, other animals can encounter the poison placed for rodents, while predators may also be exposed when they consume poisoned prey. Although the barn-nest box approach can be considered a good example of non-chemical or reduced-chemical control, it also created an ecological challenge, as owls cannot be expected to recognise the difference between an agricultural pest and a protected native rodent.This point became especially important in the northwestern Negev, a different study region from the original Beit She’an Valley experiment. The northwestern Negev’s cultivated land lies close to natural sandy habitats that support native small mammals, including several gerbil species. Researchers were stumped by the question of whether artificial nest boxes placed near these areas might increase predation pressure on species that were not agricultural targets.An unexpected pattern is revealedResearchers examined 14,632 prey items from 95 barn-owl nest boxes between 2013 and 2016 in the northwestern Negev. The study identified several protected or locally endangered rodents among the prey, including Allenby’s gerbil, the sand rat, Wagner’s gerbil and the greater Egyptian gerbil. The findings did not suggest that these endangered rodents generally dominated barn owls' diet. Instead, they constituted over 50% of the recorded prey within a specific subset of nest boxes. The pattern was especially notable at boxes located within five kilometres of sand dunes.Researchers then compared those owl-diet findings with trapping data from agricultural fields and nearby dunes, and noted that in extensive agricultural areas, Gerbillus rodents represented less than 1% of the animals caught. However, in the neighbouring dunes, gerbils were much more prominent. This data mismatch clarifies a fundamental flaw in the original 1980s deployment strategy: while boxes were placed near agricultural fields to target crop pests, their proximity to native terrain inadvertently converted a targeted biocontrol tool into a structural threat vector. Because owls selectively forage across natural habitats if nested nearby, this subpopulation of boxes installed along the desert-farm ecotone drove a massive dietary shift toward protected species, drawing apex predators directly to the borders of vulnerable conservation zones.This is a classic challenge with predator-based pest management. A barn owl does not operate according to a list of species that humans have classified as desirable or harmful. Thus, if a protected gerbil becomes accessible near a nesting territory, it can likely become a part of the owl’s diet regardless of whether or not the rodent is damaging crops.The Israeli experiment illustrated why reducing rodenticide use and protecting biodiversity cannot necessarily be treated as separate goals. While using predators can reduce reliance on poisons, predator management itself must be designed carefully when agricultural land is adjacent to conservation areas.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian drones kill 2 in Ukraine's Moldova; Zelenskyy urges stronger global response
articles.summary: Europe News: Russian strikes killed two people and injured at least four others in Ukraine on Wednesday, after a drone hit a border crossing with Moldova in the so.
articles.body: Russian strikes killed two people and injured at least four others in Ukraine on Wednesday, after a drone hit a border crossing with Moldova in the southern Odesa region and an apartment building in Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged world leaders to take stronger action against Moscow, warning that the attacks were continuing with little international response.The Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova was struck overnight, causing a major fire and forcing authorities to temporarily suspend passenger and vehicle traffic. Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said two civilians near the crossing were killed and three others were injured.Sixteen people were evacuated from the area, according to Zelenskyy. He said rescue teams were also working to deal with the aftermath of Russian attacks in the Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Zhytomyr and Kyiv regions."Unfortunately, there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes, which are taking people’s lives practically every day. But a response is needed – Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences. The aggression must be stopped here and now, before it spreads any further. And it is important that sanctions and support for Ukraine work effectively toward this goal. The partners who can help know exactly what is needed every day. And I thank everyone who is helping to the best of their ability," Zelenskyy said.In Kyiv, a Russian drone struck a 16-storey apartment building early on Wednesday, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Emergency responders were sent to the site after the strike sparked a fire.Zelenskyy said four people were injured in the attack."This morning in Kyiv, a Russian drone struck an apartment building. Four people were injured. As always, our rescuers responded swiftly, and the fire has now been extinguished. Last night in the Odesa region, the international Starokozache border crossing with Moldova was hit. Operations there have been suspended. Tragically, two people were killed and three others were injured. Sixteen people were evacuated by rescuers. My condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims. Efforts are also underway to deal with the aftermath of the Russian attack in the Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Zhytomyr, and Kyiv regions," he said.The strikes came as Russia resumed near-constant air attacks on Kyiv following a brief pause during a visit by US peace negotiators. Ukrainian officials said five people had been killed in the capital in attacks on Tuesday.The latest strikes also came amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war. On September 7, Zelenskyy said the territorial issue remained "relevant" to efforts to end the conflict. He said some of the most difficult questions could ultimately be resolved only by national leaders.Zelenskyy made the comments after talks in Kyiv with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law. He said three rounds of discussions with the US delegation had taken place and described them as substantive.Zelenskyy said he hoped the talks would help revive negotiations and lead to a lasting peace agreement.Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow welcomed Trump's efforts to bring an end to the conflict.“We welcome the efforts of American President Trump,” Peskov said.He also maintained that Russia had not wanted the war and said Moscow was seeking to end a conflict that it claimed had been started earlier.“We actually never wanted this war. What we're trying to do, we're trying to stop the war that was launched before, and it was not launched by us,” Peskov said.With Russian strikes continuing despite renewed diplomatic efforts, a lasting peace agreement between Moscow and Kyiv still appears to be a distant prospect.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Delhi mein sab chalta hai’: 2 tragedies in 3 months, questions mount over city's civic failures
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: “Delhi mein sab chalta hai,\" three months ago, those words surfaced in the aftermath of Delhi’s Malviya Nagar B&B fire — a tragedy that.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: “Delhi mein sab chalta hai," three months ago, those words surfaced in the aftermath of Delhi’s Malviya Nagar B&B fire — a tragedy that eventually claimed 23 lives.Now, after another deadly disaster in the capital, the words echo again.This time, it is not a fire but a five-storey building in Satya Niketan that came crashing down, killing seven people — five students and two labourers.Two tragedies. Two different locations. But behind both lies the same uncomfortable question: How much can be altered, ignored or allowed before a building becomes a death trap?The Malviya Nagar B&B tragedy had already exposed how far a property could drift from what it was legally meant to be.The building was more than two decades old when Lovkesh Bajaj bought it from another businessman three years earlier. Bajaj told police that the seller had suggested modifications, including increasing the size of rooms and making other alterations.The seller allegedly told him such changes were “common practice”. The consequences were deadly.The B&B had been licensed as a six-room property but had allegedly been expanded into a 25-room hotel. Investigators also found a single entry and exit point, a locked terrace and a lack of basic fire-safety systems.The chargesheet filed by Delhi Police said the accused had deliberately disregarded basic fire-safety norms and illegally expanded the property to maximise commercial returns.The June 3 blaze killed 23 people, including foreign nationals and members of an Indian family, and injured 20 others.The tragedy also exposed how quickly an illegal alteration can become a systemic failure.The building was allegedly operating across four floors, a basement and an improvised rooftop facility despite having a licence for only six rooms. It had no emergency fire exit, while the single entry and exit point meant that the same passage through which guests entered was also their only obvious route out.When the fire broke out at around 8:35 am, sleeping guests on the upper floors were caught off guard.Flames spread through combustible material, while dense black smoke travelled up the central staircase, the building’s primary passage.But the investigation that followed widened the question beyond the three people named as accused.A magisterial inquiry into the fire found regulatory failures involving multiple government agencies and said repeated opportunities to stop illegal construction and enforce safety norms had allegedly been ignored over several years.The inquiry report held the building owner and management responsible for unauthorised construction and operating without mandatory safety measures. But it also pointed to lapses by Delhi Police, the MCD, the tourism department and BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.The report said the MCD had issued stop-work notices and sought police assistance, while also asking the power company to disconnect electricity to the building. Yet the unauthorised construction allegedly continued.The police were criticised for failing to act effectively on the MCD’s notices and for not escalating the matter despite being aware of the illegal construction. The report also raised the possibility of collusion involving a beat officer.The tourism department came under scrutiny too.The B&B licence was granted despite deficiencies that, according to the inquiry, should have been apparent during inspection. The report alleged that the inspection committee failed to properly record the building’s configuration, overlooked the absence of a fire NOC and did not flag inadequate ventilation in several rooms.BRPL, too, was criticised for not acting on the request to disconnect power. In other words, the question of responsibility in Hauz Rani did not end with the owner.It moved from the kitchen to the building plan, from the building plan to the licence, from the licence to inspections, and from inspections to the agencies that were expected to enforce the rules.Three months later, the setting changed from Hauz Rani to Satya Niketan. The building came down during ongoing construction work.And once again, questions about alterations, expansion, safety and enforcement have moved to the centre of the investigation.An old building, more floors, more roomsThe Satya Niketan property was an ageing structure.According to the FIR, the owners allegedly added four floors despite knowing that the foundation could not bear the additional load. Further construction work was also allegedly underway when the building collapsed.During interrogation, Mahesh Gupta, who managed the accommodation on behalf of his parents, Hariram Gupta and Urmila Gupta, told police that the building had been leased to PG operator Hostel Daze in August 2025.Property owner Hariram Gupta, 81, is a retired Indian Air Force sergeant, while his wife, Urmila, is 75. Their son Mahesh, 52, was managing maintenance of the property, according to police.The property had been leased to business partners Shubham Tyagi and Sudhanshu, who were operating the PG facility from the premises.The labour contractor Sanoj was apprehended from Kasganj in Uttar Pradesh and brought in for questioning.The building had effectively been turned into tightly packed student accommodation.Around 15 rooms had been carved out in the 55-square-yard property, with about 45 students staying there — roughly three to a room — generating more than Rs 4 lakh a month in rent.Profit had a number attached to it. So did the risk.Repair and construction work was underway before the collapse.Mahesh reportedly told investigators that work had been underway in the basement for eight to 10 days because of the accumulation of waste and rainwater during the rainy season. The ground floor was also being repaired and expanded to increase commercial activity.Initial investigations have examined basement work, water accumulation and structural weakness as possible factors.The building, according to civic officials, dated back to the 1970s, with some repairs undertaken in 1990.An official said the property was located on a nine-metre right of way notified as a commercial street in 2007 and that the basement was constructed around that time. But the basement had no RCC pillar and was built using load-bearing walls.Investigators are now examining whether repair work on such a wall may have contributed to the collapse.That brings the investigation to another question: who approved, monitored or ignored the changes made to an ageing structure?Whom to blame? This is where the two tragedies begin to look increasingly similar. In both cases, the first instinct after the disaster was to look at the property owner and those directly operating the premises.But the blame did not stop there. In Hauz Rani, the police chargesheet focused on the owner, manager and cook. The magisterial inquiry, however, subsequently examined the role of multiple government agencies and officials.In Satya Niketan, the owners and those associated with the PG operation have been arrested. But the civic machinery is now under scrutiny as well.Three officials, two tragediesFive MCD South Zone officials were suspended a day after the collapse.They are Deputy Commissioner Rakesh Kumar, Superintending Engineer Ranvir Singh, Executive Engineer (Building) Lalit Kumar Goel, Assistant Engineer (Building) Sunil Chauhan and Junior Engineer (Building) Ashish Kumar.Three of these officials — Rakesh Kumar, Ranvir Singh and Ashish Kumar — were posted in the South Zone when the Hauz Rani fire took place, when 23 people died.No action was taken against them then. Now, after another fatal incident in the same broad civic enforcement landscape, they have been suspended.The question is not simply why action was taken. It is why it took another seven deaths.The MCD has said it has “zero tolerance” for unauthorised construction. Mayor Pravesh Wahi said the suspension of officials was aimed at setting an example and ensuring that lapses were not repeated.But the civic body itself has acknowledged that the exact cause of the collapse is still under investigation.Wahi said the building had not been classified as dangerous, although the owner was carrying out work in the basement.MCD commissioner Sanjeev Khirwar told TOI there was no confirmation of construction activity so far, but said officials had been suspended in view of local allegations and the ongoing inquiry.The distinction matters.Because if the building was not officially classified as dangerous, the question becomes whether the civic machinery had enough information to identify the risk before the structure came down.And that question becomes more uncomfortable when viewed against Delhi’s existing inspection system.The inspection paradoxThe MCD has now launched a fresh crackdown on unsafe structures.A day after the Satya Niketan tragedy, it issued show-cause notices to five buildings and a demolition notice to one in the South Zone. Several buildings around the collapsed structure were served vacation notices, while one was declared dangerous under Section 348 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act.The corporation also ordered a fresh survey of dangerous buildings in unauthorised colonies.Junior engineers in all 12 zones were asked to identify buildings that had outlived their structural life or were in a dilapidated condition and initiate action under the DMC Act.Officials were also told to ensure that owners and builders followed sanctioned building plans and complied with the applicable provisions of UBBL-2016 and MPD-2021 or MPD-2047.But the latest crackdown has also brought an earlier inspection exercise under scrutiny.The MCD building department had surveyed more than 30 lakh houses across Delhi till June-end as part of its pre-monsoon exercise.Only 51 structures were declared dangerous.Yet Satya Niketan, Hauz Rani and Said-ul-Ajaib — areas that have witnessed fatal fires and collapses — had not been declared dangerous during earlier surveys.The civic body says these surveys are based on visual inspections and complaints. Once a building is identified as dangerous, a vacation notice is served and demolition can follow.But a building does not necessarily become dangerous overnight.The more difficult question is whether years of additions, alterations, changing use and commercialisation can remain invisible until a wall cracks, a fire starts or an entire structure collapses.After every tragedy, the crackdownAfter the Satya Niketan collapse, the government has once again moved into enforcement mode.Chief minister Rekha Gupta ordered inspections of PG accommodations and action against illegal construction. She also ordered immediate sealing of buildings with unauthorised fifth floors.The government has also ordered inspections of nearby PGs and buildings.On September 8, the civic body surveyed 1,150 PG accommodations housing around 20,000 people, examining structural and fire-safety concerns.The LG and CM also discussed the safety and accommodation of students living in PGs. The chief secretary was directed to ensure that structural audits of buildings in major PG hubs were completed within a week.But LG T S Sandhu also cautioned against indiscriminate sealing drives, warning that such action could leave students homeless. A committee was asked to reach out to students living in PGs, hear their grievances and prepare a comprehensive database.The government is also examining alternative student accommodation through universities, the MCD and the DDA, including the possibility of using vacant and unutilised buildings owned by the two agencies.At the same time, the Delhi Disaster Management Authority control room and emergency contact numbers were ordered to be made operational.The measures are immediate. The problem is not.Who owns the building — and who is responsible for what happens inside it?Satya Niketan has also exposed a regulatory grey area around basements and structural alterations.Civic officials say permission for a basement is granted by the concerned urban local body, and the basement forms part of the sanctioned building plan. Construction has to comply with the applicable provisions of the Master Plan and building regulations.For plots up to 500 square metres, empanelled professionals have prescribed certification and inspection responsibilities, while the civic body retains a statutory role in monitoring compliance.Mandatory clearances and safety requirements, including fire and structural safety provisions, have to be complied with before and during construction, depending on the nature of the work.Any basement built without permission or modified in violation of the sanctioned plan can invite action.But the question in Satya Niketan is not simply whether rules exist.It is whether anyone was checking.A citywide problem, not a single buildingThe Satya Niketan collapse is not an isolated building story. Delhi Fire Service data show that more than 330 building-related calls were received between January 1 and September 6 this year. Such incidents left 30 people dead and 120 injured.The corresponding period last year saw 446 such calls, with 46 deaths or fatal incidents and 155 injuries.The calls include not just major collapses but also complaints and precautionary calls involving cracks, falling bricks, roof collapses and other building-related concerns.Delhi has already witnessed the Said-ul-Ajaib collapse on May 30, which killed six people, as well as building collapses in Malka Ganj’s Sabzi Mandi area and Karawal Nagar in June.The Hauz Rani fire came in the middle of that pattern. Satya Niketan has now added another seven deaths.And the problem extends beyond Delhi. Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 33,000 people died across India in incidents involving building collapses, fires and falls into pits and manholes, according to government data.Experts say the numbers point to a wider problem of urban governance, maintenance and enforcement.Former urban development secretary M Ramachandran said accountability needed to exist at every level — from councillors and municipal officers to mayors.PSN Rao, dean of the School of Planning and Architecture, said municipal authorities already have laws and rules that need to be enforced. Regular inspections of potentially dangerous buildings, he said, are a basic municipal responsibility.A retired civil servant who worked in the urban development ministry and held senior positions in states also pointed to a lack of supervision and monitoring.The problem, experts said, is not necessarily the absence of rules or even manpower. It is whether the system acts before something goes wrong.And whether officials are willing to stop construction, seal a property or force an owner to undo an illegal alteration before the building becomes a headline.The redevelopment excuse — and the counter-claimAfter Satya Niketan, another layer was added to the blame game.MCD officials attributed unchecked vertical expansion in resettlement colonies, including Satya Niketan, to the absence of a clear redevelopment policy.They argued that such colonies did not receive the same redevelopment benefits available to other residential areas under MPD-2021, where buildings can have a permissible height of up to 17.5 metres.According to civic officials, this had created space for illegal vertical expansion over the years.They also pointed out that PGs and hostels can operate on residential plots under mixed-use regulations, subject to prescribed road-width and other conditions. But in some resettlement colonies, buildings stand on narrow roads and were originally designed as much smaller structures.The buildings, officials said, often have load-bearing walls rather than RCC columns.That makes unauthorised structural alterations particularly risky.One MCD official said standard building plans in resettlement colonies had permitted ground-floor construction with limited first-floor development. Such planned structures, officials said, are now difficult to find because buildings have expanded vertically without the required approvals.MCD also argued that the problem is not confined to one colony.Similar patterns can be seen in areas such as Madanpur Khadar, Mangolpuri and Trilokpuri, where plots can be as small as 25 square yards.DDA, however, pushed back against the suggestion that the absence of a redevelopment policy explains the problem.It pointed to Clause 4.5.4(i)(c) of MPD-2047, which provides for redevelopment of resettlement colonies under regeneration schemes.But DDA also acknowledged that every development or construction still requires a building plan to be sanctioned by the concerned local body.That leaves the central question unresolved.If the rules require sanction, who ensured that the construction remained within those rules?The Hauz Rani inquiry showed what happens when responsibility is divided across agencies: the owner can be blamed for illegal construction, the operator for running the premises, officials for failing to enforce rules, departments for overlooking deficiencies and utility agencies for failing to act on warnings.Satya Niketan is now raising the same question in a different form.The arrests have begun.The suspensions have begun.The inspections have begun.The demolition notices have begun.The policy announcements have begun.But accountability cannot begin and end with the first action after a tragedy.Because by then, the people who needed protection have already paid the price. Delhi has heard the phrase before: “Delhi mein sab chalta hai.”It may explain how an extra floor, an extra room, an unauthorised alteration or a commercial use survives for years.But it cannot explain why the system waits for 23 deaths in a fire — and then seven more in a collapse — before asking who was watching.The real question is no longer whether “sab chalta hai”. articles.title: 'Allies should stand with us': Congress calls out Abdullahs after full version of Vande Mataram played
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Congress has urged its allies to “stand with us” in singing a shorter version of Vande Mataram, after all six stanzas of the national s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress has urged its allies to “stand with us” in singing a shorter version of Vande Mataram, after all six stanzas of the national song were played at an event attended by Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah and his father, Farooq Abdullah, the top two leaders of Congress ally National Conference (NC).Congress general secretary (organisation) KC Venugopal argued that the full version of Vande Mataram “sits uneasily with the syncretic and pluralist ethos that our freedom fighters envisioned and nurtured for India.”“For us, the considered judgment of Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Nehru, Sardar Patel, Subhash Chandra Bose, Rajendra Prasad, Acharya Narendra Dev, Maulana Azad, Sarojini Naidu and J.B. Kripalani — shaped in no small part by the counsel of Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore — remains paramount,” Venugopal said on X.“With respect and humility, we would like our allies to honour the wisdom and judgment of our freedom fighters, and stand with us in singing only the version of this beautiful and historic song that they adopted,” he added.The Alappuzha MP maintained that the Congress' decision to sing only the first two stanzas was made “deliberately” to prevent the song from being “communalised." He was referring to the Congress’ 1937 resolution recommending that only the first two stanzas of the national song be sung to “maintain communal harmony."In July, the BJP-led Centre enacted the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026, granting Vande Mataram statutory protection on par with the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. The law mandates the singing of the full version at official events and provides for imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both for anyone found guilty of “insulting” the song.On August 15, Vande Mataram was played for the first time at the official Independence Day ceremony. It was played in full before and after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s address to the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort in Delhi.Accused of "minority appeasement" by the ruling BJP, the Congress has stood its ground, repeatedly invoking the 1937 resolution to justify singing only the first two stanzas.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Poster-boy actions': Vijay Mallya's message to those calling him 'bhagoda'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Vijay Mallya said he is legally barred from leaving the UK, claiming his innocence on Wednesday, in a series of posts on X.The allegedly fu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Vijay Mallya said he is legally barred from leaving the UK, claiming his innocence on Wednesday, in a series of posts on X.The allegedly fugitive businessman has claimed that the Indian Government has been grossly unjust to him."For all who say I am a bhagoda refusing to come to India, please be aware that I have been a permanent resident of the United Kingdom since 1992 and am currently legally prohibited from leaving this country. All this started with poster-boy actions by the Government of India who have been grossly unjust in my case," Mallya said in his post.In October 2025, Mallya was among the list of 15 high-profile names that were declared Fugitive Economic Offenders (FEOs) under the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 (FEOA). He shares the list with Nirav Modi.In a separate post on Tuesday, Mallya referred to an alleged Enforcement Directorate affidavit purportedly filed before the Bombay High Court, claiming it showed recovery of Rs 14,131.60 crore from him in 2021."Para 7 is the decreed debt and Para 17 shows recovered Rs 14,131.60 crore in 2021!! 5 years on I am still referred to as a fraud who cheated the Banks," he wrote.He also shared what he described as an account statement of recoveries, questioning why he continued to be labelled a fraudster and asking when he might receive a refund. Mallya further claimed that the ED had released over Rs 350 crore from his attached funds to pay Kingfisher Airlines employees, asserting he had been unable to make those payments himself because his assets had been frozen.This is not the first time Mallya has made such claims. In August, he wrote on X that banks and the government had "admitted" to recovering Rs 14,100 crore from him against a judgment debt of Rs 6,203 crore, contrasting this with settlements reached by other borrowers "at a fraction" of what they owed.The Centre, for its part, reiterated in December last year that it remained committed to bringing economic offenders back to face trial, though the ministry of external affairs acknowledged that "several layers of legalities" were involved in such cases.Mallya's claims come against the backdrop of an ongoing legal battle, where he challenged the constitutional validity of the Fugitive Act and the proceedings under which he was declared a fugitive.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: California removed more than 900,000 pounds of human debris while restoring 40 acres; crews deliberately left old telephone poles because purple martins can use them as nesting sites
articles.summary: US News: California crews left old telephone poles standing while restoring about 40 acres of land at Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve because purple martins us.
articles.body: California crews left old telephone poles standing while restoring about 40 acres of land at Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve because purple martins use holes in the poles as nesting sites. The decision came as part of a wider restoration project in which more than 900,000 pounds of human debris was removed from the newly acquired properties.The Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District recently completed the restoration work on several properties that were added to the preserve. According to it, the land had abandoned vehicles, dilapidated structures and other debris accumulated over the years.While most of these remains were removed, the old telephone poles were kept. Midpen staff had discovered purple martins nesting in holes inside similar poles near the mountain top while working on Mount Umunhum.The discovery was significant because purple martins were thought to have disappeared from Santa Clara County. The western subspecies, Progne subis arboricola, prefers natural structures such as cavities in standing dead trees, known as snags. The birds found in Sierra Azul were using the old telephone poles in a similar way.Purple martins' nestsPurple martins are migratory birds that typically spend winters in South America before returning to North America in summer to breed. During these months, they need suitable nesting places as well as areas with flying insects for food.The western purple martin is different from the more common eastern variety in its choice of nesting sites. Eastern purple martins primarily rely on nest boxes supplied by humans, while the western subspecies prefers more natural cavities.Competition from nonnative European starlings for suitable nesting sites had led biologists to believe that the western purple martin was close to local extinction. Finding the birds nesting in Sierra Azul therefore led Midpen to begin efforts to support the population.The district started a multiyear programme to monitor the birds and test different nesting options. Its first attempt involved installing nest boxes, which had attracted purple martins in Oregon and Washington. However, the box-style design did not attract nesting birds in Sierra Azul.Midpen then designed a hollowed wooden pole that was intended to mimic the cavities found in natural structures. The design took into account the cavity dimensions, entrance-hole size and the height of the opening above the ground.The approach eventually showed results. In 2022, purple martins were confirmed nesting for the first time in the new Midpen-built structures. The finding supported the idea that western purple martins prefer more natural nesting habitats.'Ecological well-being of the land'The restoration project also focused on clearing the wider landscape of human debris. Crews removed more than 900,000 pounds of material from the approximately 40 acres incorporated into Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve.Some of the waste required special handling. Teams removed and disposed of building materials containing lead and asbestos, along with old septic systems. This was done to protect restoration workers and prevent pollutants from entering the local watershed.After the debris was removed, specialists re-graded the land to resemble its natural, pre-development slopes. This was intended to restore the area's original drainage patterns.The final stage involved hand-seeding the land and spreading weed-free straw to support the return of native chaparral and forest.“Our goal is to work in a way that supports the ecological well-being of the land,” said Midpen Capital Project Manager Ayden Sabharwal.The restoration is also connected to the planned Umunhum-to-the-Sea regional trail. The properties are located along the future trail corridor.Meanwhile, Midpen plans to continue monitoring the purple martins and work with partner agencies to share expertise on habitat improvements.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1977, two young travelers reached an abandoned Belize farm only by canoe; their 140 acres eventually grew into a 400-acre private jungle reserve
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the journey of Mick and Lucy Fleming as they transformed a 140-acre abandoned farm into a thriving 400-acre private jungle reserve in Belize, known as Chaa Creek. Learn about their farming, eco-tourism, and commitment to conservation.
articles.body: Mick and Lucy Fleming came to Belize in 1977 and found themselves living on an overgrown 140-acre farm along the Macal River in the country's Cayo District. The couple used a dugout canoe to transport produce to San Ignacio as they began farming the land.According to Chaa Creek's official history, the Flemings grew vegetables, raised animals and produced food such as milk and eggs after they settled on the property. They spent the first years in developing the farm rather than running a resort, eventually began receiving visitors, and became one of Belize's early jungle lodges.The farm became a place for travelers to stayChaa Creek's timeline records that the couple purchased 137 freehold acres in 1981 and built the first Chaa Creek cottage that same year. A second cottage came in 1982, while two more A-frame cottages and a dining room were added in 1983. The road that connected the property to the outside world was also constructed that year.Electricity did not reach the kitchen until 1987, and the lodge's history records the installation of hot water in the rooms in 1988. The operation expanded gradually, with nature activities and additional cottages added during the following years. A separate account published by Chaa Creek in 2021 describes the reserve as part of the same gradual expansion. The Flemings began to develop around the existing trees rather than clearing the property wholesale, and the farm eventually evolved into a larger conservation and tourism operation.Land was added around the original farmChaa Creek's own environmental account says the private nature reserve eventually reached 400 acres. Other additions recorded in the company's history included the purchase of Penades Land, which is a 65-acre parcel, and Joe Cal's Land, another 13 acres, in the early 1990s. The timeline also records the purchase of a 65-acre Maya farm in 1999 and other parcels in later years.The original farm had become a much larger landscape that contained accommodation, agricultural areas, trails and forest. Farming remained part of the operation, while the surrounding forest became an increasingly important part of the visitor experience. A dataset held by the Global Biodiversity Information Facility and associated with the University of Belize's Environmental Research Institute describes Chaa Creek as a privately owned eco-lodge situated on a 400-acre private nature reserve along the Macal River, and also includes bird surveys conducted in the area between 1997 and 2001.The reserve became part of the lodge's identityChaa Creek also developed a Natural History Centre and butterfly facilities, and turned parts of the property into places for environmental and educational activities. The lodge's own history records the Natural History Centre being built in 1995, and the Macal River Camp was established in 1997, while later additions included a trail system for hiking and horseback riding and a butterfly farm.The University of Belize-linked bird dataset records that point-count surveys were conducted along transects at the property, and observers documented bird species and numbers at repeated sampling points. The researchers described the reserve as consisting largely of secondary forest and open areas, surrounded by pasture and agricultural land.The land developed from a farm into a lodge, while additional acreage and surrounding forest became part of a private reserve used for conservation, tourism and research. Chaa Creek's own website describes the reserve as larger than the 400-acre figure used in its earlier material, but the 400-acre description remains documented in the property's historical accounts and biodiversity records. The original 1977 farm, meanwhile, is still identified as the starting point of the operation. The route that once required a dugout canoe is now part of a developed lodge and nature reserve in western Belize, but the Macal River remains central to the property that the Flemings first reached in the late 1970s.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Human rights organisations condemn 'racist murder' of Manipuri singer Chongtham Vikram in Delhi
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A group of civil society and human rights organisations has condemned the death of Manipuri music teacher and singer Chongtham Vikram, who .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A group of civil society and human rights organisations has condemned the death of Manipuri music teacher and singer Chongtham Vikram, who was allegedly killed by a mob in Delhi on Monday. The group called for a thorough probe into the possible racial motive behind the attack.The joint statement was issued after a meeting of the Manipur Students’ Association Delhi (MSAD), Manipur International Youth Centre (MIYC), People’s Progressive Alliance Manipur (PPAM), Karwan-e-Mohabbat (KeM), North East India Support Centre and Helpline (NEISCH) and Human Rights Alert (HRA) on September 8 at the Centre for Equity Studies in Sarvodaya Enclave, New Delhi.The groups said Vikram's murder should not be treated as an isolated criminal incident. They said it must be examined in the wider context of racial prejudice and violence faced by people from Northeast India.The statement said an FIR, numbered 0296, has been registered at Sunlight Colony police station under Sections 103(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.Section 103(2) deals with murder committed by a group of five or more people acting together on grounds including race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief. Section 3(5) provides for joint liability when several people commit a criminal act in furtherance of a common intention.The organisations said the police investigation so far appeared inadequate to address what they described as a broader pattern of racist crimes against people from the Northeast.They also pointed to the recommendations of the MP Bezbaruah Committee, which was set up by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs and submitted its report in 2014. The committee had recommended measures to tackle discrimination, violence and the vulnerabilities faced by people from Northeast India.The groups said most of those recommendations, including a proposal to specifically criminalise racist acts, remain unimplemented.They also highlighted the absence of a comprehensive legal framework dealing specifically with racial discrimination. The statement noted that Article 15 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination on several grounds but does not expressly list colour, descent, national origin or ethnic origin.The organisations further cited recommendations issued by the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) on August 25, 2026. They urged the Centre to adopt comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation with a clear definition of racial discrimination, covering both direct and intersecting forms of discrimination in public and private spheres.The groups demanded an impartial and transparent investigation into Vikram's death, including an evidence-based examination of any racial motive.They also called for all those responsible to be identified and prosecuted, including anyone who may have participated in, facilitated or encouraged the attack.The organisations urged authorities to ensure that the case is not investigated merely as an ordinary criminal offence without considering its alleged racial dimensions.They also sought immediate measures to prevent further racist violence against people from Northeast India, along with institutional mechanisms to tackle racial discrimination and hate-based violence.The groups called for support, protection and compensation for Vikram's family and urged authorities to protect them from intimidation, harassment or further victimisation.The statement said, "Justice for Chongtham Vikram is not merely a demand for accountability for one murder. It is a demand for dignity, equality, security, and the fundamental right to live free from racial violence for all people from Northeast India."The meeting ended with a two-minute silence in memory of Vikram and in solidarity with his bereaved family.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
